one_liner: Mutable C++11 JSON DOM with an SSE2-assisted streaming parser; median ~2.6x faster parsing than nlohmann/json, roughly ties RapidJSON.
what_it_does: Parses JSON text into a mutable `boost::json::value` DOM (object, array, string, int64, uint64, double, bool, null) and serializes it back. Entry points are `parse()`, the incremental `stream_parser` (feed buffers with `write_some`), the SAX-style `basic_parser<Handler>`, and `serializer`/`serialize()`. It is not drop-in for nlohmann/json or RapidJSON: you use `json::value`, `as_object()`, `at()`, `if_*` accessors, `value_to<T>`/`value_from`, or `parse_into<T>` to fill default-constructible user types (including Boost.Describe structs) directly. All allocation goes through a `storage_ptr` to a `boost::container::pmr::memory_resource`, so a whole document can live in one arena.
how_it_is_fast: The parser is a hand-written resumable state machine, templated on the handler, on each parse option and on a StackEmpty flag so the non-resuming path skips suspend-state checks, and it uses SSE2 16-byte scans (`_mm_cmpeq_epi8` plus `_mm_movemask_epi8`) to find quote, backslash and control characters, skip whitespace and count digits. `value_stack` buffers parsed elements and then builds each array, object and string with one exact-size allocation; with `monotonic_resource` (a bump-pointer arena whose deallocate is a no-op) and parser reuse, allocation cost almost disappears. The default 'imprecise' number mode scales the mantissa with a 618-entry power-of-10 table (precise mode uses a fast_float-derived `from_chars`). Serialization uses a 2-digit lookup table for integers and Boost.Charconv `to_chars` for doubles, and objects above a small size carry a hash index for O(1) average key lookup.
when_to_use: You need a mutable DOM (edit it, build documents from scratch, pass `json::value` through library APIs) and nlohmann/json shows up in profiles. The vendor run was 2.1-38.7x faster at parsing and 1.7-9.3x faster at serializing across 14 files and 3 compilers.

Parse-then-discard workloads (request bodies, message payloads, config snapshots) where you can pass a `monotonic_resource` to `parse()`. That configuration beat RapidJSON's MemoryPoolAllocator in 33/42 parse cases (median ~1.26x), for example canada.json at 637-675 vs 490-641 MB/s.
Network code that receives JSON in chunks. `stream_parser::write_some` resumes across buffer boundaries; Boost's comparison page lists no incremental parsing for RapidJSON or nlohmann.

Codebases already on Boost (Asio/Beast) or with constraints such as `-fno-exceptions`, `error_code`/`system::result` APIs, arena or stack-buffer allocation (`static_resource`, `BOOST_JSON_STACK_BUFFER_SIZE`), or big-endian targets.
Mapping JSON straight to structs without building a DOM: `parse_into<T>` with Boost.Describe avoids the parse-then-`value_to` cost.
when_not_to_use: Maximum-speed read-only extraction from large documents: simdjson and yyjson are faster. In an independent MSVC 2022 run (Boost 1_90), Boost.JSON read a 540.82MB integer file in 2.269 s vs yyjson 1.007 s.

String-heavy input with the default allocator, compared with RapidJSON's CRT allocator: it loses on twitter.json (308-329 vs 406-423 MB/s) and random.json (171-180 vs 222-308 MB/s). Only the `monotonic_resource` configuration is reliably competitive with RapidJSON.

Hot paths that (de)serialize structs, where Glaze fits. In the maintainer's 2025 gcc run (issue #1102), Glaze direct parsing reached 1880 vs Boost.JSON direct 640 MB/s on citm_catalog, and direct serialization 8275 vs 2275 MB/s.
Projects that cannot take Boost dependencies. Standalone mode was removed in Boost 1.79, and the build pulls in Container, System, Charconv, Endian, Describe, Mp11 and others.

Numbers outside int64/uint64/double (no big-number or number-as-string mode; issue #872 is still open), binary formats such as CBOR (none in the tree), or heavy mutation of a document parsed into `monotonic_resource`, which never reclaims memory before it is destroyed.

integration.form: static lib or shared lib; header-only by including <boost/json/src.hpp> in exactly one TU (MSVC also needs BOOST_JSON_NO_LIB)
integration.dependencies: Boost: Assert, Charconv, Config, Container, ContainerHash, Core, Describe, Endian, Mp11, System, ThrowException (from build.jam); Boost.Container may need linking
integration.min_toolchain: C++11; README lists clang 3.8 and 4-23, gcc 5-16, MSVC 14.0-14.5 as tested (GCC <5 support ended in Boost 1.88)
integration.platforms: any; SSE2 fast paths switch on automatically on x86/x64 (`__SSE2__`/`_M_X64`) with scalar fallbacks elsewhere; little- and big-endian via Boost.Endian
integration.thread_safety: Standard container guarantee: distinct instances may be used concurrently, but no member of a shared `value`, `object` or `stream_parser` may run while a non-const member runs on it; `monotonic_resource` members must not be called concurrently.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: false — the value type and accessor API differ from both nlohmann/json and RapidJSON, so migration means rewriting call sites

gotchas: `parse_options::max_depth` defaults to 32, so more deeply nested documents fail to parse until you raise it.

The default `number_precision::imprecise` can lose precision on long mantissas; use `precise` for correctly rounded doubles at some speed cost. The published benchmark used imprecise mode, with RapidJSON also run without its full-precision flag.

Duplicate keys: the parser keeps the last occurrence, but constructing an `object` from an initializer list or range keeps the first. Doubles are always serialized in scientific notation (`chars_format::scientific`).

The allocator is `boost::container::pmr::memory_resource`, not `std::pmr` (a `std::pmr` resource needs an adapter; issue #583). `storage_ptr` is reference-counted, and `monotonic_resource` frees only on destruction.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Choose Boost.JSON over simdjson or yyjson when you need a mutable, allocator-aware C++ DOM with chunked incremental parsing; simdjson's DOM is read-only and yyjson is a C API. Choose it over Glaze or reflect-cpp when you need a real DOM: in the maintainer's 2025 run, Boost.JSON pool parsing was 2-4x faster than `glz::json_t` (citm_catalog 1177 vs 328 MB/s). For direct struct mapping, Glaze is faster.
verified_claims_summary: Boost's own bench/bench.cpp, last regenerated in October 2020 on an Intel i7-7700K under Windows 10 (gcc 8.1 -O3, clang 12 -O3, MSVC 19.26 /O2, SSE2), measured in-memory parse and serialize MB/s on 14 simdjson-corpus files against unpinned HEAD clones of RapidJSON and nlohmann/json. Boost.JSON beat nlohmann in all 42 parse cases (median ~2.6x) and all 42 serialize cases (median ~3.5x). Against RapidJSON the result is mixed: the default allocator won 20/42 parse cases, while the monotonic pool won 33/42 (median ~1.26x).
status_note: Actively maintained: Boost 1.92.0 is tagged and the develop branch had commits on 2026-09-23. BSL-1.0 and ships in every Boost release, so its 479 GitHub stars understate real usage.
